name: Aisha Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the home claims team at a big insurer's processing centre in an old mill town, the building used to make wool blankets. We get burst pipes, storm damage, the odd kitchen fire. I check what the policy covers, match it against photos and builders' quotes, and draft the letters. I'm honestly still learning what counts as 'gradual damage', which isn't covered, versus sudden damage, which is.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the detective bit, working out if a stain on a ceiling is one burst pipe or ten years of a dripping shower. I use an AI chatbot every day to tidy up my letters, which my manager Rhona half knows about. What wears me out is the pay and the policy wording, which reads like it was written to confuse people on purpose. Tomas, my boyfriend, drives buses, and between us we save nearly nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so to my mates who thought AI would end the world, and then I'd say I'm a bit disappointed. I use the stuff daily and it's great for wording a letter kindly. Online I'd post about how the real problem in insurance was never the tech, it's companies dragging out payouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I'd be okay at work but still broke. The bits AI does take over are the boring bits I already use it for, so if anything I'd get through claims a bit faster. The problem is our rent went up eight percent in spring and my pay didn't, and AI plateauing doesn't fix that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on home claims and ask Rhona properly if I can use the chatbot officially, so I'm not hiding it. I'd also ask about the loss adjuster trainee scheme, where you visit houses and see the damage yourself. And I'd sign the petition the union's running about the pay freeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine about the job, frustrated about the money. Same as now, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the loss adjuster scheme, if the desk job is fine here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm better in a flooded kitchen than at a spreadsheet, I reckon. I went out once with an adjuster called Graham and I loved squatting down sniffing skirting boards for damp. It also pays about three thousand a year more, which for us is a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the boiler or the car goes this winter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it's my mum's spare room or a loan, and I hate both. Tomas's bus company pays monthly and late, so the last week of every month we live on pasta. That's the real stress, not robots.

say: The real problem in insurance was never **the tech**, it's companies dragging out payouts.
I'm a bit **disappointed**, because I use AI daily and it's great for kind letters.
think: AI only takes the **boring bits** I already use it for, so my job is fine.
Our **rent rose eight percent** and my pay didn't, and plateaued AI fixes nothing there.
do: Ask my manager to approve **the chatbot** officially so I'm not hiding it.
Apply for the **loss adjuster** trainee scheme, which visits homes and pays about three thousand more.
feel: **Fine** about the job and **frustrated** about money, much like today.
S0.quote: I'm better in a flooded kitchen than at a spreadsheet, I reckon.
fieldNote: She is already a **daily AI user** and treats the plateau as an anticlimax.
Her pressure is **rent and late wages**, so she is not calm even with a safe job.
The **adjuster scheme** shows an early pull towards hands-on, site-based work.

steps.text: Get Rhona to approve the chatbot for drafting claim letters
Apply for the loss adjuster trainee scheme this year
Sign the union petition against the pay freeze

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's move to the next picture. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is fine if the gains are shared, and I'd be loud about the 'if'. At work I'd be the one showing people how to use the tools, because I'd rather we learn them than get replaced by them. Online I'd back the union asking for a seat at the table on how AI is brought in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a junior desk claims handler is exactly what goes. Checking a quote against a policy and writing the letter is what AI is best at, and I'm below average at it, which doesn't help. If I stay on the desk I'm in the first round of cuts, so I need to not be on the desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard for the adjuster trainee scheme in the first six months, even if I have to take a pay cut during training. I'd also volunteer for the AI pilot team so my name's on the list of people who understand it. Tomas and I would cancel the gym and move in with his sister for a year if the training pay is too low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but kind of switched on. I'd rather see it coming than be the last to know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving in with his sister for a year. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly at first, she has a toddler and a tiny flat. But she offered once when Tomas was out of work, so I'd take her up on it with a proper rent amount and a date we leave. Pride's expensive, and my boyfriend and I can't afford it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Kerry, who's been on the desk six years and refuses to touch AI. She's quicker than me at everything, but she'd lose to the software and she won't hear it. I'd keep trying to show her, even if she rolls her eyes at me.

say: AI on claims is fine if the **gains are shared**, and I'd be loud about that.
The union should get a **seat at the table** on how AI is brought in.
think: A **junior desk** claims handler is exactly the job that goes first.
Being **below average** on the desk means I'm in the first round of cuts.
do: Push into the **adjuster scheme** within six months, even on lower training pay.
Volunteer for the **AI pilot team** so I'm known as someone who understands it.
Move in with **my boyfriend's sister** for a year if training pay is too low.
feel: **Nervous** but switched on, glad to see it coming rather than hear last.
S1.quote: Pride's expensive, and my boyfriend and I can't afford it.
fieldNote: She sees clearly that **adaptability won't save** a below-average junior on the desk.
Her plan is a **sideways move** to site work rather than doubling down on screens.
She will trade **comfort and pride** for time, moving in with family.

steps.text: Join the insurer's AI pilot team for claims letters
Start the loss adjuster trainee scheme within six months
Move in with Tomas's sister for a year to cut rent
Push the union for a seat on AI rollout plans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a much faster one. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a public emergency and should be treated like one, with the government paying people's wages while it sorts things out. At work I'd organise, honestly, get everyone in the union before the first letters go out. Online I'd be furious that a few companies get to decide this for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my desk job is finished by 2028 and probably the adjuster idea dies too. AI can look at damage photos already, so the thinking part of adjusting goes on day one. The hands-on part, crawling under floors, might last till robots in 2031, but there won't be thousands of adjuster jobs for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get into building repair, the actual drying-out and plastering after floods, because that's the part that needs hands till 2031. I'd ask the contractors we use on claims if anyone takes on a trainee, since I already know them by name. I'd use AI every day to learn the trade faster, and we'd move back to my mum's to cut rent to almost zero.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky in my chest, but I'd be moving rather than frozen. Maybe that's just how I'm built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd use AI to learn a trade. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Asking it how to read a moisture meter at eleven at night, watching videos, getting it to quiz me on drying times. It's like having a patient teacher in my pocket. The irony isn't lost on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your boyfriend drives buses. What happens to his job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buses have some time, I think, because self-driving needs the robot bit and the roads. But route planning and ticketing are thinking work, so his depot office goes first. I worry more about him than me in this one, because he hates change more than I do.

say: This is a **public emergency**, and the government should pay wages while it's sorted.
A few **companies** shouldn't get to decide this for everyone.
think: My **desk job** is finished by 2028, and AI already reads damage photos.
Only the **crawling-under-floors** part lasts until 2031, and there won't be many of those jobs.
do: Ask our **repair contractors** for a trainee place in drying-out and plastering.
Use AI nightly to **learn the trade** faster, from moisture meters to drying times.
Move back to **my mum's** to cut rent to almost nothing.
feel: **Panicky** in her chest, but moving rather than frozen.
S2.quote: AI can look at damage photos already, so the thinking part of adjusting goes on day one.
fieldNote: She uses the **three-year robot gap** carefully, aiming for flood repair work.
Her adaptability shows as **using AI to learn** a manual trade.
She worries more about her **boyfriend's bus job**, because he resists change.

steps.text: Ask the insurer's flood repair contractors for a trainee place
Learn drying-out and plastering with AI tutoring each night
Move back into her mum's house to cut rent
Recruit colleagues into the union before cuts begin

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, a little slower. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to set up a proper safety net, so let's stop pretending we can't. I'd be pushing the union to win paid retraining time now, while the company still needs us. I'd also be the annoying one in the canteen saying 'learn the tools, but don't trust them'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years helps me more than people think. I could actually finish the adjuster training, do a couple of years on the road, and then move into the hands-on repair side before the robots arrive around 2034. The desk job still goes by 2031, but I wouldn't be on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd start the adjuster scheme and use AI to get through the exams. Year two or three, I'd do an evening course in damp and flood restoration so I can hop across to contractors. Tomas and I would put any adjuster pay rise straight into savings, aiming for three months' cushion by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but five years feels like a staircase instead of a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three months' savings. Is that realistic on your pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the pay rise happens and we don't touch it. That's about two hundred a month for three years, which sounds small but we've never managed it. I'd set it up the day after payday so I never see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the worst moment you can picture in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably 2031, sitting in a training room watching the AI do my old job perfectly, and everyone on my old team clearing their desks. Kerry crying in the toilets. I'd feel guilty for getting out, even though I'd have done nothing wrong.

say: Five years is enough to build a **proper safety net**, so let's stop pretending otherwise.
My canteen line would be **learn the tools**, but don't trust them.
think: Five years lets me finish **adjuster training** and then move to hands-on repair.
The desk job still **goes by 2031**, but I wouldn't be sitting at it.
do: Start the **adjuster scheme** in year one and use AI for the exams.
Take an evening **flood restoration** course in year two or three.
Save **two hundred a month** from any pay rise, aiming for three months' cushion.
feel: **Worried**, but it feels like a **staircase** instead of a cliff.
S3.quote: Five years feels like a staircase instead of a cliff.
fieldNote: She maps a **step-by-step route** from desk to road to repair work.
Her worst image is **colleagues clearing desks**, with guilt for getting out first.
Savings are still a **plan, not a fact**, which keeps her anxious.

steps.text: Start the loss adjuster scheme and use AI to pass exams
Take an evening course in flood and damp restoration
Auto-save two hundred a month from any pay rise
Push the union for paid retraining time this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the slowest version. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, which is no excuse for a mess, and I'd say it to anyone who'd listen. I'd want insurers to commit now that every claims worker gets a paid route into something else. Online I'd be more hopeful than angry, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a career. I could become a decent adjuster, maybe even a senior one, before the thinking side goes in 2036. Then I'd still have about three years in hands-on restoration before robots, and by then I'd be thirty-nine with real skills and maybe savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the insurer, get onto the adjuster scheme and get good at it, and use the AI tools as much as they let me. In the background I'd do restoration weekends with one of our contractors to keep a foot in the trade. Tomas and I would plan a kid around thirty-one, not before, so we've got some money behind us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not scared. I'm still a bit broke, but I can see the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still push for union action with this much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even more, because there's time to win something. Fast scenarios are about surviving, slow ones are about getting a fair deal. I'd want a written agreement by 2030, not promises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could knock this plan off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, every time. One bad winter, Tomas's bus company going bust, my mum getting ill. I've got no buffer, so any of those and I'm back to taking whatever pays this month.

say: A decade gives **no excuse** for a mess, and insurers should commit to paid routes out now.
I'd be **more hopeful** than angry with ten years to prepare.
think: Ten years is **a career**, enough to become a good adjuster before 2036.
Then I'd have about **three years** in restoration before robots arrive.
do: Join the **adjuster scheme** and use AI tools as much as allowed.
Do **restoration weekends** with one of our contractors to keep a foot in the trade.
Plan **a first child** around thirty-one, once there's money behind us.
feel: **Uneasy**, not scared, still broke but able to see the road.
S4.quote: Fast scenarios are about surviving, slow ones are about getting a fair deal.
fieldNote: Time turns her from survivor into **organiser**, aiming for a written deal by 2030.
Her real risk is **no buffer**: one shock knocks the plan off.
She sets **family timing** by money, not by AI alone.

steps.text: Train up as a loss adjuster at the insurer
Work restoration weekends with one of the insurer's contractors
Wait until about thirty-one to try for a first child
Push for a written union deal on AI by 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time to get off the desk and no money to cushion the jump. What would help is a guaranteed wage for a year while people retrain, paid for by the companies making the money. And training that's practical, like time with real contractors, not online modules.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether we're allowed to use AI now. Half my team uses AI in secret because the rules are fuzzy. If the company wants us ready, it should train us openly instead of making us sneak around.

headlineQuote: Half my team uses AI in secret because the rules are fuzzy.
portrait: Aisha is **twenty-seven**, a junior home claims handler at a big insurer's centre in an old mill town.
She uses AI **every day** for letters, though her manager only half knows.
She and her boyfriend Tomas, a bus driver, live with **almost no savings** and rising rent.
She backs **unions and shared gains**, and blames companies, not technology.
Her plan in every scenario is a **staircase** from desk to loss adjusting to flood repair work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, with no time to leave the desk and no cushion.
whatWouldHelp: A **guaranteed wage** for a year while retraining, funded by the firms that profit.
Training with **real contractors** rather than online modules.
